Literally, "Nor of men (have we been found, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.5">1Th 2:5</reference>) seeking glory." The "of" here represents a different Greek word from "of" in the clause "of you ... of others." Alford makes the former (Greek, "ex") express the abstract ground of the glory; the latter (apo) the concrete object from which it was to come. The former means "originating from"; the latter means "on the part of." Many teach heretical novelties, though not for fain, yet for "glory." Paul and his associates were free even from this motive [Grotius], (<reference osisRef="John.5.44">Joh 5:44</reference>).<div eID="gen36637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we might have been burdensome--</hi>that is, by claiming maintenance (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.9">2Co 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.16">12:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.8">2Th 3:8</reference>). As, however, "glory" precedes, as well as "covetousness," the reference cannot be restricted to the latter, though I think it is not excluded. Translate, "when we might have borne heavily upon you," by pressing you with the weight of self-glorifying authority, and with the burden of our sustenance. Thus the antithesis is appropriate in the words following, "But we were gentle (the opposite of pressing weightily) among you" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.7">1Th 2:7</reference>). On weight being connected with authority, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.10">2Co 10:10</reference>, "His letters are weighty" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.21">1Co 4:21</reference>). Alford's translation, which excludes reference to his right of claiming maintenance ("when we might have stood on our dignity"), seems to me disproved by <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9">1Th 2:9</reference>, which uses the same Greek word unequivocally for "chargeable."
